title: Bartimaeus (Mark 10:32–52)
hookLine: a blind beggar shouts louder when told to be quiet, and is asked what do you want
tomorrow: the fig tree and the temple

lines: WON'T TAKE NO FOR AN ANSWER.
A BLIND MAN BEGINS TO SHOUT.
cards: Some people won't take no for an answer. Today, one of them is the hero. Jesus is on the road to Jerusalem, walking out in front, and his followers are amazed and afraid.
He tells them a third time what will happen there. Then they pass through Jericho, on the way up to the city, with a big crowd. By the side of the road, begging, sits a blind man named Bartimaeus.
He hears it's Jesus of Nazareth passing by. And he starts to shout.

teach.h: JAMES AND JOHN WANT THE BEST SEATS.
teach.b: First, the question before him. Just before Jericho, James and John ask Jesus for a favor, and he asks them: what do you want me to do for you? They want the seats of honor, at his right and his left, in his glory.
He tells them the Son of man "is not come to be ministered unto, but to minister, and to give his life a redemption for many." Hold on to that question. Second, the shout.

teach.h: SON OF DAVID, HAVE MERCY ON ME.
teach.b: Bartimaeus cries, in the Douay-Rheims: "Jesus son of David, have mercy on me." Son of David is a royal title, a king's name. The crowd tells him to be quiet.
He shouts louder. Third, the call. Jesus stops: call him.
Suddenly the same crowd is kind: "Be of better comfort: arise, he calleth thee."
Bartimaeus throws off his cloak and leaps up. Remember yesterday's rich man, who couldn't let go of his possessions.

teach.h: THE SAME QUESTION: WHAT DO YOU WANT?
teach.b: Fourth, the same question. "What wilt thou that I should do to thee?" Nearly word for word what he asked James and John.

Bartimaeus says: "Rabboni, that I may see." Jesus tells him his faith has made him whole; he sees, and Mark says he followed him on the way. Mark gives his name and his father's: Bartimaeus, son of Timaeus.
Some readers wonder whether Mark's first readers knew him. And his cry, have mercy on me, echoes in the Jesus Prayer, prayed by Eastern Christians and by Catholics too.

how: Some Catholics pray the Jesus Prayer, a short cry for mercy that echoes Bartimaeus, repeated slowly with the breath or on a prayer rope.

he names him: Bartimaeus, the son of Timaeus.

games.q: you're Bartimaeus, blind by the road. Jesus is passing, and the crowd tells you to be quiet. what do you do?
o: go quiet and hope he notices.
ask someone to lead you to him.
games.why: he cried a great deal more, "son of David, have mercy on me." Jesus stopped and called him.

practice: Imagine Jesus stopping on the road, turning, and asking you what he asked Bartimaeus: what wilt thou that I should do to thee?
Answer in one quiet sentence, not with what you think you're supposed to want but with what you actually want, small or enormous.
If you pray, say it to him as your prayer; if you don't, just notice what came up, and how it felt to name it.
